## Executive Summary {#executive-summary}

This analysis looks at the housing quality of renters throughout New York City through the lens
of racial equity. Our primary goal was to answer the question, “controlling for other predictor,
how different is the number of housing issues across different races?” We already know that
Black and Hispanic New Yorkers are overrepresented in public and subsidized housing
throughout the city, but we hope to identify if there are differences in housing quality that are not
explained by external factors such as housing subsidy or building age. If race itself is a predictor
of housing quality, then it is possible that some other form of housing discrimination, whether it
be historic, systemic, or explicit, is still impacting New Yorkers today and will likely require
direct intervention and legislative solutions to ensure equity for all New Yorkers.

## Methodology {#methodology}

This analysis uses the 2023 New York City Hosing Vacancy Survey (NYCHVS), a triennial
survey conducted by the U.S. Census Bureau on behalf of the New York City Department of
Housing Preservation and Development. The NYCHVS is the primary source for housing
conditions data in New York City and includes information on renter characteristics, building
characteristics, subsidy program participation, and physical housing conditions. Survey
responses were collected January through mid-June of 2023. The 2023 NYCHVS had a sample
of about 15,600 housing units and a response rate of 71% percent (weighted response rate: 68%).
Each unit in the 2023 NYCHVS dataset represents approximately 385 similar housing units.
The analytic sample for our models is drawn from the full NYCHVS renter file and split into
three subsamples for analysis: subsidized renters (public housing, voucher holders, and other
subsidy programs; n=1,125), unsubsidized renters (n=1,973), and all renters combined
(n=3,098). A survey weighted negative binomial model using the 80 replicate weights from the
NYCHVS was run for each of the three analytic subsamples. Variance estimation uses the
NYCHVS successive difference replication (SDR) method, in which 80 replicate weights (FW1–
FW80) are used to compute standard errors via the formula: Var = (4/80) × Σ(theta_r − theta_0)².
The outcome for each of the three models was the count of unique serious unsafe housing
conditions.2 Housing quality issues are self-identified by renters in the NYCHVS. Our analysis
controlled for race3, subsidy program4, rent regulation program5, building information6, and
household demographics including if the presence of children, older adults, and single adult
households.

## Policy Implications {#policy-implications}

Together these findings seem to suggest that external factors alone such as building age, rent
regulation status, and housing subsidy status do not explain all of the differences in housing
quality across different racial groups. Even after accounting for these factors, Black and Hispanic
renters report significantly more housing issues than White renters with otherwise similar
housing situations. This points to some form of housing discrimination (historic, systemic, or
explicit) that continues to affect New Yorkers today. Legislative solutions should prioritize
identifying where in the rental process these issues are arising. Some examples of this could be:

• Reporting bills that evaluate whether existing housing discrimination protections (e.g.,
source-of-income protections, fair housing enforcement) adequately address disparities
that persist after controlling for subsidy and regulation status
• Reporting bill to require a matched-audit study of rental applications or analysis linking
housing conditions to historic redlining maps, to identify where in the housing pipeline
these disparities originate.

Possible mechanisms of housing discrimination including historic redlining, differential
application approval by race, or neighborhood-priority policies that make it harder for Black and
Hispanic New Yorkers to move into higher-quality-housing neighborhoods, remain untested by
this analysis and are worth further study. But the disparities themselves are not in question: they
are statistically significant, hold across subsidized and unsubsidized renters alike, and are not
explained by the factors this analysis controls for.
